evidence.claim: A pipeline haul road crosses the Yukon and the Brooks Range
evidence.quote: the Dalton was originally developed as a haul road connecting the Yukon River and Prudhoe Bay during construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

evidence.claim: A pipeline haul road crosses the Yukon and the Brooks Range
evidence.quote: the only road in the United States to cross the Yukon River, Arctic Circle, and Brooks Range.

evidence.claim: The Dalton Highway runs 414 miles from the Elliott Highway north of Fairbanks to Deadhorse, near the Arctic Ocean.
evidence.quote: is a 414-mile (666 km) road in Alaska. It begins at the Elliott Highway, north of Fairbanks, and ends at Deadhorse

evidence.claim: Much of the drive is on gravel, with several steep grades.
evidence.quote: The Dalton Highway is mostly a gravel road with several steep grades.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s transportation department includes it among the state’s scenic byways and highlights a combination unique to a U.S. road: crossings of the Yukon River, Arctic Circle and Brooks Range.
evidence.quote: DOT&PF / DMIO / Alaska's Scenic Byways / Dalton Highway

evidence.claim: crossings of the Yukon River, Arctic Circle and Brooks Range
evidence.quote: the only road in the United States to cross the Yukon River, Arctic Circle, and Brooks Range.

evidence.claim: Built in 1974 to supply construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System, the road took its name from Arctic engineer James W. Dalton.
evidence.quote: it was built as a supply road to support the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System in 1974. It is named after James W. Dalton

evidence.claim: Crews completed 390 miles in five months; the pipeline followed in 1977.
evidence.quote: Within 5 months, 390 miles (630 km) of the road were built and construction was finished. The pipeline would not be completed until 1977.

evidence.claim: Public access came in stages, reaching Disaster Creek in 1981.
evidence.quote: In 1981, the highway was opened to the public up to Disaster Creek at mile 211.

evidence.claim: An Alaska Supreme Court decision ordered removal of the permit requirement in 1993, and the full highway opened to the general public on December 2, 1994.
evidence.quote: The Alaska Supreme Court overruled the 1991 decision in 1993, ordering the state to remove the permit requirement. The permit system was eliminated and the full length of the highway was opened to the general public on December 2, 1994.

evidence.claim: Arctic engineer James W. Dalton
evidence.quote: as an expert in Arctic engineering

evidence.claim: Heading north, cross the Yukon before reaching Coldfoot and Wiseman.
evidence.quote: Fuel is available at the E. L. Patton Yukon River Bridge (Mile 56), as well as Coldfoot and Deadhorse.

evidence.claim: The highway follows the Dietrich River for 25 miles, then crosses the Continental Divide at Atigun Pass.
evidence.quote: The Dalton Highway ascends the Dietrich River valley and follows the river for 25 miles.

evidence.claim: Beyond the Brooks Range, Slope Mountain marks the gateway to the treeless coastal plain on the way to Deadhorse.
evidence.quote: Look for Dall Sheep on Slope Mountain, gateway to the treeless coastal plain.

evidence.claim: Heading north, cross the Yukon before reaching Coldfoot and Wiseman.
evidence.quote: Coldfoot (pop. 34) at Mile 175, Wiseman (pop. 12) at Mile 188

evidence.claim: then crosses the Continental Divide at Atigun Pass.
evidence.quote: It is where the Dalton Highway crosses the Continental Divide (at mile marker 244)

evidence.claim: on the way to Deadhorse
evidence.quote: at the end of the highway at Mile 414

evidence.claim: At the Yukon crossing, look for the pipeline crossing the river beside the highway.
evidence.quote: At first sight of the Yukon River, look for the Pipeline crossing the Yukon

evidence.claim: The Yukon River Bridge carries both the Dalton Highway and the pipeline, the only bridge crossing of the Yukon in Alaska.
evidence.quote: The bridge carries both the Dalton Highway and the Alaska Pipeline in connecting Fairbanks with Deadhorse near the Arctic Ocean and the Prudhoe Bay Oil Field. It is the only bridge crossing of the Yukon in Alaska.

evidence.claim: A permanent crossing was needed to complete the pipeline project.
evidence.quote: a permanent crossing of the Yukon River became necessary in order to complete the project.

evidence.claim: The October 1975 ribbon-cutting allowed Alyeska to use the unfinished span and avoid building an ice bridge that winter.
evidence.quote: Although still not yet complete at the time, the bridge celebrated its ceremonial ribbon-cutting on October 10, 1975. This allowed Alyeska to start using the span, thus eliminating the need to construct an ice bridge that winter

evidence.claim: Its driving surface is timber, supported by a steel deck and two steel box girders.
evidence.quote: The driving surface of the span is of timber construction supported by a steel deck attached to a pair of steel box girders.

evidence.claim: In 1982, the state named it for Edward Patton, Alyeska’s former president during pipeline construction.
evidence.quote: In March 1982, the state officially named the bridge in honor of Edward Patton, former president of the Alyeska Pipeline Service Company during construction of the pipeline.

evidence.claim: Coldfoot began as a mining camp called Slate Creek.
evidence.quote: The town was originally a mining camp named Slate Creek

evidence.claim: In 1902 it had two roadhouses, two stores, seven saloons and a gambling house.
evidence.quote: In 1902, Coldfoot had two roadhouses, two stores, seven saloons, and a gambling house.

evidence.claim: Its post office closed in 1912 and reopened in 1984.
evidence.quote: A post office operated from 1902 to 1912, then reopened in 1984.

evidence.claim: The town now primarily serves as a Dalton Highway truck stop.
evidence.quote: Coldfoot primarily serves as a truck stop on the Dalton Highway

evidence.claim: Its overnight quarters include converted pipeline construction camp accommodation.
evidence.quote: a small number of overnight accommodations (converted pipeline construction camp quarters).

evidence.claim: That working-road role extends to an Alaska transportation department maintenance station.
evidence.quote: The Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities (DOT&PF) has a camp (maintenance station) in Coldfoot.

evidence.claim: The next services north are in Deadhorse, 240 miles away.
evidence.quote: North of Coldfoot, there are no services for 240 miles (400 km), until Deadhorse.

evidence.claim: Atigun Pass takes the Dalton Highway across the Continental Divide at mile 244.
evidence.quote: It is where the Dalton Highway crosses the Continental Divide (at mile marker 244)

evidence.claim: At the head of the Dietrich River, this is the only pass through the Brooks Range crossed by a road.
evidence.quote: located at the head of the Dietrich River.

evidence.claim: Alaska’s transportation department identifies a turnout at the summit.
evidence.quote: Take advantage of the turnout at the summit of Atigun Pass.

evidence.claim: The pass is maintained throughout the year, but winter brings avalanches.
evidence.quote: is the highest pass in Alaska that is maintained throughout the year.

evidence.claim: Farther north, the route reaches the treeless coastal plain at Slope Mountain.
evidence.quote: Look for Dall Sheep on Slope Mountain, gateway to the treeless coastal plain.

evidence.claim: the only pass through the Brooks Range crossed by a road.
evidence.quote: Atigun is the only pass in the Brooks Range that is crossed by a road.

evidence.claim: winter brings avalanches.
evidence.quote: is also home to avalanches during the winter.

evidence.claim: North of Wiseman, the route passes Gates of the Arctic National Park to the west and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to the east before reaching the pass.
evidence.quote: North of Wiseman, you will pass by Gates of Arctic National Park to the west and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to the east.

evidence.claim: near the Arctic Ocean.
evidence.quote: near the Arctic Ocean and the Prudhoe Bay Oil Fields.

evidence.claim: The wooden deck has been replaced several times, including in 2007.
evidence.quote: The wooden deck has been replaced in 1981, 1992, 1999 and 2007.

evidence.claim: A small summer visitor center brings together staff from the Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service and National Park Service.
evidence.quote: The BLM, USFWS, and NPS jointly staff a small visitor center during the summer.
